answer.exemplar: Fusion of light nuclei releases energy only once the nuclei get close enough for the short-range nuclear force to bind them, and the electric repulsion between the positive charges is what stands in the way. Turning the repulsion into kinetic energy means an energy of order 1 MeV per pair, which corresponds to a temperature of order 1e10 K, far above anything a container can hold. The way round this is to compress the fuel until the density itself supplies the pressure, or to use a charged particle so that electric fields can confine and compress it, which is why a working fusion reactor is both extremely dense and extremely hot at the same time. Two further points matter. The energy is released only after the barrier is crossed, so a modest temperature produces nothing at all, and because the products are less massive than the reactants the reaction is self-sustaining at a high temperature, whereas a fission chain dies away if the temperature falls. A good answer should also note that the barrier gets taller as the charges increase, so fusing two deuterons is harder to achieve than the deuterium-tritium reaction with one proton in the pair.

questions.explanation: Each fission releases a few neutrons, and on average some fraction of them go on to cause another fission. A steady state requires the multiplication factor to be exactly one, so that the number of fissions in one generation equals that in the next and the power neither rises nor dies away. If the factor were above one the population and the temperature would run away, and if it were below one the reaction would stop. The balance is delicate because the fraction of neutrons that cause fission depends on their energy, which is why a reactor contains both a material that leaks neutrons away and a material that slows them down to the energy where fission is most likely. Only about one neutron in ten from a fission actually causes another fission, the rest being absorbed or lost.

questions.explanation: Fission is far more likely for a slow neutron than for a fast one, because the slow neutron is more easily captured by the nucleus and has time to be drawn in by the nuclear force. Neutrons born in a fission are fast, so a thermal reactor puts material in the fuel to slow them by elastic collisions with light nuclei, which is why graphite, water and heavy water are used and why ordinary water works for the common reactor types. A fast reactor deliberately skips this stage and uses a fuel that fissions efficiently with fast neutrons, so the moderator is a design choice rather than a necessity. Getting the speed right is only half the job, since the neutrons must still be allowed to reach a fuel nucleus, which is the work of the control rods and of the core design.

answer.exemplar: The water round a core does two separate jobs, and it is worth keeping them apart. As a moderator it slows the fast neutrons born in fission by elastic collisions with the light nuclei of the water, so that they reach the thermal energy at which a fuel nucleus is most likely to capture them, and that is what allows the chain reaction to sustain itself. As a coolant it removes the heat from the fuel, which is essential in its own right, because a nuclear reaction does not stop when it gets hot: the rate rises with temperature unless the moderator geometry changes too, which is the positive temperature coefficient that makes a light-water reactor self-regulating to a large extent. A good answer should also note the trade-off, since a moderator that is good at slowing neutrons is not necessarily a good absorber of them, and that a reactor using a solid moderator such as graphite needs a separate coolant. The arrangement of fuel rods, moderator and coolant is what sets the size of the positive temperature coefficient, and that number is the practical measure of how safe a design is.

questions.explanation: A good answer separates the two effects. The first is moderation: neutrons produced by fission are fast, and they are slowed by elastic collisions with the light nuclei of the water until they have the thermal energy at which a uranium nucleus is most likely to capture them, so without this the chain reaction would not sustain itself. The second is cooling: the fuel gets very hot and has to shed that heat, and the water carries it to the steam generator. The two are linked by a useful accident, since water is densest and least compressible when cold, so a rise in temperature makes the moderator less effective and tends to shut the reaction down rather than let it run away. A reactor with a solid moderator such as graphite still needs a coolant, and a reactor with a hot moderator has to be designed with a smaller positive temperature coefficient, which is why the geometry of the fuel and the coolant is safety critical.
questions.hint: Separate what the water does to the neutrons from what it does to the heat.

questions.explanation: The chain begins with capture, because until a neutron is absorbed the nucleus is stable and nothing else can occur. The capture leaves the nucleus in an excited state, and the split into two fragments follows, which is what produces both the energy and the new neutrons. The fragments then fly apart and their energy is converted into heat in the fuel and coolant. Only after that are the released neutrons slowed by elastic collisions in the moderator, and finally one of those slowed neutrons is absorbed by another fuel nucleus, which closes the generation. Two orderings are worth rejecting explicitly: the slowing cannot precede the release, because the neutrons have to exist first, and the heat cannot appear before the split, because the fragments carry the energy.

answer.exemplar: The date marks the moment the tree stopped exchanging carbon with the atmosphere. While a tree is alive it is taking in carbon dioxide, and it builds its wood with the same proportion of carbon-14 to carbon-12 as the atmosphere, because the carbon-14 in the atmosphere is continually replenished by cosmic ray production. When the tree dies, or when a branch is cut, or when a piece of bark is replaced, that exchange stops, the intake of fresh carbon-14 ceases, and the carbon-14 already present simply decays away at its half-life. The measurement therefore dates the cessation of growth, not the germination of the tree, so a date on a wooden beam refers to the felling and a date on a ring boundary refers to the year that ring finished. It also explains why an old building gives a spread of dates: different timbers were felled at different times and may have been reused from an earlier structure, so a cluster of dates is a stronger claim than a single date.

questions.explanation: The date refers to the point at which the tree stopped taking in fresh carbon, not to the moment the seed germinated. A living tree keeps its carbon-14 proportion in step with the atmosphere, so its wood looks like the atmosphere, and once the tree is dead, or a branch dies, or bark is shed, the replacement tissue begins to lose carbon-14 with a half-life of 5730 years. A beam of structural timber therefore dates the felling of the tree, which can be a century or more after germination, and a ring dated directly gives the year that ring closed. Different dates from one building are expected for several reasons: the timbers were cut at different times, they came from trees of different ages, and old beams are commonly reused from earlier structures. A tight cluster of dates is thus much stronger evidence than a single date.

answer.exemplar: A Geiger-Muller tube works by avalanche. A single ionising particle creates a few thousand ion pairs, and the resulting avalanche is so large that the whole tube discharges, so the output pulse size says nothing about how much energy the original particle carried. What the counter reports is therefore the number of pulses, not the number of particles. Every pulse takes a fixed time to complete and is followed by a recovery period during which the tube voltage is too low for a new avalanche to be triggered, and that dead time is of order a hundred microseconds. When the source is weak the arrivals are far apart and each one is counted. When the source is strong enough that two particles arrive inside one dead time, the second is missed entirely and the count rate saturates at the reciprocal of the dead time, whatever the true activity becomes. A good answer should also say that this is why the counter is moved further away for a strong source, since the correction must be made geometrically and the meter itself cannot be trusted once it is saturated, and why readings are quoted in counts per second rather than in becquerels without a calibration.

questions.explanation: A good answer starts with the avalanche. One ionising particle creates a few thousand ion pairs in the tube, the discharge that follows is the same size whatever caused it, and the pulse is followed by a recovery period of order a hundred microseconds during which the tube cannot respond again. That recovery period, the dead time, means two particles arriving close together are counted as one. When the arrival rate rises until the average interval between particles is comparable with the dead time, further increases in the activity simply add particles that arrive during a dead interval and are lost, so the reading flattens out at a limit set by the tube and not by the source. The consequences matter for measurement: a saturated counter under-reports, so a strong source is counted from further away or through extra shielding, and a reading in counts per second only becomes an activity in decays per second after a calibration that is valid while the tube is responding linearly.

The result is a dense trail of ion pairs in a single cell and a high local dose, and once the source is inside the body those alpha particles are delivered directly to the tissue with nothing left to stop them. A gamma ray of the same energy passes straight through the body, so its energy is spread over a large volume and much of it escapes without depositing anything. The two sources having equal activity only fixes the rate of decay, not the damage, because the hazard depends on the energy absorbed per unit mass. This is why alpha-emitting materials are handled with such care and why an inhaled or ingested alpha emitter is a far more serious contamination than an external gamma source of the same strength.
